areas.key_indicators: Revised vision, mission and values (Nov 2025); 5 strategic objectives; CAPEX program PhP 255.4 M (2026–2029)
findings: New vision: world-class, sustainable waterworks with 24/7 potable supply by 2035.
Five objectives defined: billed volume, NRW, collection, cost recovery, after-sales service.
Three priority projects: pipe replacement (PhP 113.1 M), coverage expansion (PhP 22.9 M), new main lines for bulk water (PhP 119.4 M).
Plan is preliminary; objectives lack owners, annual targets and timelines.
areas.message: Clear direction is in place; objectives now need owners, annual targets and deadlines to become an executable plan.

areas.key_indicators: Tariff PhP 6.20/m3 vs PhP 17.68/m3 cost-recovery tariff (2024); collection efficiency not measured; metered connections not reported
findings: 6,461 connections (2024), 98.9% residential; average consumption 26.1 m3/connection/month.
Tariff unchanged at PhP 6.20/m3 (2020–2023); it should be PhP 17.68/m3 to recover OPEX.
Collection efficiency is not calculated; no baseline exists.
Meters are purchased by customers and are not always replaced when required.
Online payment partners are already available.
areas.message: The tariff is about one-third of cost and collection is not measured; the revenue base is the critical constraint.

areas.key_indicators: NRW 31.3% (Level 1); NRW 16.2 l/conn/h (Level 3); continuity 22–24 h/day (Level 4); availability 180 l/cap/day (Level 4)
findings: Production 7.66 MLD vs billed 5.26 MLD: about 2.4 MLD lost every day.
Supply is reliable (22–24 h) from deep wells with chlorination at all pump stations.
Old galvanized iron pipes in Tiptip, Manga and Ubujan; no DMAs yet; no preventive maintenance.
Supply gap of 11.7 MLD against projected city demand.
areas.message: Continuity is good, but one-third of produced water is lost; cutting NRW is the cheapest source of new supply.

findings: Water sales PhP 22.9 M (2024) vs OPEX PhP 26.1 M (2023): operating loss of about PhP 3.2 M.
Negative bottom line acknowledged by the utility.
Operates as a Local Economic Enterprise (LEE), not funded by the general fund; accounts not yet ring-fenced.
Proposed tariff (PhP 214.03 for the first 10 m3) makes the plan financially viable and affordable (2% of low-income household income).
areas.message: Revenues do not cover operating costs; tariff reform and ring-fenced LEE accounts are required for cost recovery.

areas.key_indicators: 9 regular staff + 15 job-order (24 total, 6 female); 1.39 regular staff per 1,000 connections (Level 5); 3.7 including job-order
findings: Lean staffing ratio, well below the 1:250 industry average.
Heavy reliance on job-order staff (63% of workforce).
Multi-tasking of personnel and unclear organizational structure.
Training needs in technical, finance, billing and collection, management and water safety planning.
No data on turnover or HR costs.
areas.message: The team is lean and committed but stretched; formalize the structure and invest in technical, finance and billing skills.

findings: 10% of samples fail national drinking water standards (PNSDW).
Chlorinators installed in all pump stations.
Water quality monitoring and compliance identified as a weakness.
areas.message: Disinfection is in place, but a 10% sample failure rate requires a water safety plan and stronger monitoring.

areas.key_indicators: Water coverage 27% of city population (Level 1); approx. 33% of households in the 10 served barangays
findings: Serves 10 of 15 barangays; other providers (BWUI, Richli) supply most of the city.
Expansion to Cabawan, Booy, Cogon, Dampas and Bool planned; 11,908 households to benefit by 2039.
TCWS does not provide sanitation services.
areas.message: Coverage is low even inside its own service area; expansion depends on new supply and investment.

areas.key_indicators: 9 of 22 performance indicators can be calculated; preliminary KPI system defined
findings: No data on collection, metering, customer satisfaction, complaints, turnover or HR costs.
Annual OPEX and production volumes for 2024 not available.
A preliminary KPI monitoring system with standards and frequencies has been defined.
areas.message: Most performance gaps cannot be measured yet; establishing baselines is the first step.

messages.text: TCWS provides reliable water to its customers but is not financially sustainable: the tariff covers about one-third of cost, one-third of water is lost, and revenues fall short of operating costs.
Average performance level across the 9 measurable indicators: 2.8 of 5 (between Basic and Good).
Raise revenue: adjust the tariff toward cost recovery, linked to visible service improvements.
Reduce NRW from 31% to 20% through DMAs, pipe replacement and control of illegal connections.
Measure what matters: set baselines for collection, metering and customer service.
Ring-fence the waterworks account and assign owners and deadlines to each objective.
Build staff capacity in technical operations, finance, billing and water safety.

strengths.text: Already a Local Economic Enterprise (LEE), not funded by the general fund
Chlorinators installed in all pumping stations
Responsive team, especially in emergency services
Reliable supply of 22–24 hours per day
Lean staffing ratio (1.4 regular staff per 1,000 connections)

weaknesses.text: Old galvanized iron pipes (parts of Tiptip, Manga, Ubujan)
Need for training of technical and finance personnel
Lack of training for billing and collection, management and water safety plans
Water quality monitoring and compliance (10% failure in sampling)
High NRW (31%) and no district metered areas
Collection efficiency and metering not measured

opportunities.text: Availability of bulk water supply in a few years
NGOs and private organizations that help improve water services (e.g., USAID, Maynilad)
Support from other local water utilities (collaboration with BWUI)
Proposed tariff is financially viable and affordable (2% of low-income household income)
Expansion to 5 unserved barangays; 11,908 households to benefit by 2039
City commitment to digitalize billing and keep TCWS public

threats.text: Natural hazards such as typhoons and earthquakes (standby gensets in selected pump stations)
Deep well sources of private institutions, establishments and businesses
Competition from other water providers in the city (BWUI, Richli)
Rising electricity costs (power is the largest projected OPEX item)
Customer resistance to tariff increases without visible service improvement

review_notes: Coverage needs reconciliation: the Coverage & Inclusion assessment states 27% of city population, while the SWOT weakness states 24%. Confirm the reporting period and population denominator. Financial findings compare 2024 revenue with 2023 operating expenses; tariff viability and affordability statements are preliminary assessments, not independently verified results.
